newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour tax to hit water, power firms most - IFS.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour tax to hit water, power firms most - IFS.

text.p: British opposition Labour party's proposals for a windfall levy on privatised British utilities are likely to hit water and electricity firms most, the Institute of Fiscal Studies (IFS) said on Wednesday.
"The probable base would use a measure of excess shareholder returns. This would tend to shift the burden of the tax towards the water and electricity companies," the IFS said.
Labour plans to raise around 3.0 billion stg from a tax on utilities to cover the cost of the welfare-to-work scheme if it wins the May 1 election.
The IFS warned that if markets were not convinced that the tax was a one-off, there could be worries about the stability of the tax and regulatory regime, possibly increasing the cost of capital.
"This would be likely to feed through into higher prices at the next regulatory review and might also reduce the amount of investment carried out by the firms."
The IFS said the tax could result in inequity because some of the shareholders who would have to shoulder the tax might not have benefited from low issue prices.

"One worrying aspect of the tax is that it demonstrates the trend towards seeking tax increases that can be presented easily, rather than those that are most desirable economically," said Lucy Chennells, the author of the IFS report.

The IFS said Labour's announcement on the windfall tax suggested it was likely to be levied upon the regional electricity companies, the water and sewerage companies, the electricity generators and the national grid, as well as British Gas, British Telecom and the British Airports Authority.
It said more recently privatised companies such as Railtrack and British Energy might also be included if the tax base runs up to the present.
